cd /home/claude && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='SLICE-13-READINESS-SCOPE.md'
s=open(p).read()

# R2 becomes a required build item, not conditional
old_start = s.find("## R2 — Item Groups · IN FLIGHT · owner: CC + Vu")
old_end = s.find("## R3 — Unresolved leaves")
new_r2 = """## R2 — Item Groups · **REQUIRED FOR 1.0** · owner: CC + Vu

**Edward's directive: item grouping must work for 1.0.** This is not conditional on how the backfill resolves — it is a build item, and there are three routes to it. None are blocked.

**Why it matters:** the Item Group is why a customer invoice shows one turnkey line instead of freight, customs, and setup as separate lines. **Customer-visible, not cosmetic.** Today Aisha wraps them by hand.

### What's proven

`POST bare group → GET expanded lines → PATCH each member rate` **works** (Probe 7). Prerequisite: every group member needs an item-level `price`, and **`$0.00` satisfies the validator** — which is semantically correct here, since DPS builds custom products and doesn't know a price until supplier costing returns.

Also proven dead, so nobody re-litigates: group-at-create-time is refused by **both REST and SOAP**, and by **PATCH** as well as POST (Probes 5, 6, 7). Same validator, same error, every payload shape.

### The route depends on one unknown

**Does the HubSpot→NetSuite sync propagate `hs_price` to items that ALREADY EXIST in NetSuite, or only on creation?**

Vu's finding relocated the fix: NetSuite items are unpriced because the **HubSpot products** are unpriced. The sync carries what exists upstream. But if it's create-only, a HubSpot backfill never reaches the 937 existing items.

**CC's five-row test answers this.** Set `hs_price = 0` on five products, record the timestamp, poll the NetSuite items, report propagation time — or its absence.

### Three routes, all viable

| Route | When | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **A — HubSpot backfill** | Sync propagates to existing items | Cheapest. Backfill, rebuild the payload. Days. |
| **B — Vu updates NetSuite directly** | Sync is create-only | Vu offered and can bulk-update. Sidesteps the sync. **Also set HubSpot** so new items carry it forward. |
| **C — SuiteScript RESTlet** | Both above fail | ~60 LOC + deployment + a NetSuite-side ownership handoff. Previously rejected on ownership grounds; that objection is weaker now grouping is required. |

**Recommendation if the sync is create-only: do A and B together.** HubSpot for future correctness, NetSuite for the existing 937. One round trip instead of two.

### Work items

1. CC Stages 1–2 — assess + rollback capture (read-only)
2. **Five-row test** — picks the route
3. Backfill per the chosen route, with Stage 4 safeguards: filter to unpriced **at read time**, re-query immediately before executing, assert counts match, stop on discrepancy
4. `mapLeafToHubspotCreate` writes `hs_price: 0` — **stops the trickle at source**
5. Products created directly in HubSpot outside Nexus — needs a HubSpot-side default, or confirmation it doesn't happen
6. Rebuild the grouped-SO payload in `sales-orders.ts`

### Two hazards — now REQUIREMENTS, not cautions

These were "design against" when grouping was optional. Grouping is required, and it lands on the irreversible step.

**H1 — Sublist PATCH returns 204 while silently duplicating.** `PATCH /salesOrder/{id}` with a full `item.items` array **appends a second group expansion**. Doubled rollup. **No error.** A wrong Sales Order that reports as successful.
→ **Must be structurally impossible in the code, not avoided by convention.** Only `PATCH /salesOrder/{id}/item/{lineIdx}` with `{rate: X}` is safe.

**H2 — Partial failure mid-sequence.** The write is now `POST → GET → N × PATCH`. A crash between PATCHes leaves the SO created, group expanded, **some members priced and some at $0** — a valid NetSuite record with wrong amounts, and nothing flags it.
→ **Read-back verification before marking the push succeeded:** re-read the transaction lines, confirm every expanded member carries its intended rate, and only then write `netsuite_so_pushes.status='succeeded'`. Rollback via SO delete on mismatch.

**Per-SO call count goes from 1 to 8–12.** More failure surface on the one action that cannot be undone. The retry path must converge without duplicating — same discipline as #145.

"""
s = s[:old_start] + new_r2 + s[old_end:]

# Update the "why this exists" framing
s = s.replace(
"**If this doesn't resolve:** the manual wrap is a permanent stated limitation someone signs off on knowingly — not a footnote.\n\n---\n\n", "")

open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PYEOF

input.file_text:
# Slice 14 — Launch Readiness

**Status:** proposed
**Date:** 2026-07-28
**Author:** CA
**Depends on:** Slice 13 closing

---

## Why this exists

Slice 12 builds the mechanism. Slice 13 makes it work end to end without intervention. **Slice 14 makes it something a team can actually use.**

Different output, different audience, and — for the first time in this project — **the audience is PMs, not agents.**

**Cannot start before Slice 13 closes.** If Item Groups resolve, the send flow changes. Training written against a moving system gets written twice.

---

## L1 — Full lifecycle smoke

Everything walked so far has been step-scoped: Step 7's reversibility, 8b's receipt, 8c-4's send. **This is the whole application in one pass.**

**Coverage:**
- Setup → Costs → Pricing → Preview → Send → Client Review → Acceptance → Sales Order
- Revise from sent · revise from accepted · rollback · version compare
- Every failure state: below floor, unmatched leaf, unmapped customer, NetSuite push failure
- The `complete` state and its freeze

**Setup and Costs have not been walked since Slice 11.** Everything downstream changed underneath them.

**Run by CB, independently.** Track record across this slice: 10 findings on Step 7, 7 on 8b, 6 on 8c-4 — each after CC's own suites came back green. This is the highest-yield verification available.

**Also required:** a **second pass by a real PM**, not CB. Different failure mode — CB finds contradictions and broken logic; a PM finds things that are technically correct and practically unusable.

---

## L2 — Backlog burn-down

**First task: CC produces the actual list.** The items below are what CA tracked; the real backlog is larger.

### Known, from Slice 12

| Item | Origin | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **Customer PDF: Tier 2 unit prices render as em dash** | 8c-4 fixture walk | **Blocker** — customer-facing quote with missing prices |
| **Customer PDF: inconsistent money formatting** (`$20.00` vs `$100`) | same | High — customer-facing |
| **Customer PDF: PREPARED FOR / PREPARED BY overflow** | same | Medium — triggers on long legal names |
| **Pattern 52 freeze never smoke-verified** | 8c-3 | High — implemented but unproven; Clerk blocked the test, not the freeze |
| **Classifier config validation** (`floor > target` makes `BELOW_FLOOR` unreachable) | 8c-3 smoke | Medium — silent guard failure |
| **Two retry buttons in the failed state** | CB, flagged twice | Low — R9 canonical, but a repeated usability signal |
| **`drizzle/manual/` vs auto-tracked numbering collision** | #145 | Low — grep-hostile |
| **CB bug 5: spontaneous navigation to `?tab=tier`** | Step 7 walk | **Re-check** — believed harness-side, but that tab is now irreversible |
| **Orphan SO after a tier change mid-retry** | 8c-4 idempotency trace | Medium — semantically correct, but leaves an unreferenced SO |
| **`business_segment` enum→label resolver** | 8c-2 | Low — deferred, needed if the SO segment field is ever populated |

### Also
- Whatever Step 10's CD designer audit surfaces
- Whatever Slice 13's production smoke surfaces
- Legacy data: the Epicuren 6-version copy-flow chain (five orphaned drafts, `isCurrent` on v1)
- **MS OAuth** — pending IT. Blocks team sign-in and CB self-authentication.

---

## L3 — Training & enablement

**The first workstream whose audience is PMs.**

**Deliverables:**
- Written modules covering the full lifecycle, by task rather than by screen
- Presentation for the team rollout
- A short reference for the failure cases — what "unmatched leaf" means, who fixes it, what to do while waiting
- Something for Aisha and accounting on what changes for them

### Treat the writing as a review pass

**If a step is hard to explain, it is usually hard to do.** Writing "here's how you send an order" reliably surfaces steps that don't survive explanation.

**File what surfaces as findings, not as documentation friction.** This is the last review the system gets before real users, and it's a different lens than any agent has applied.

### Sequencing
Written **after** Slice 13 closes, so the flow is stable. Reviewed by someone who didn't build it.

---

## L4 — Launch prep

- **SPEC compliance audit** (carried from the original v1 plan)
- **Full automated test pass**
- **Pre-launch data cleanup** — sample-seed leaves (`LIB-`, `LEAF-GLW-`, `Nexus-Smoke-Test-1`, `TEST-LFC2-*`), throwaway quotes, orphaned drafts
- **Production credential verification** — NetSuite and HubSpot, production scope, smoke-tested
- **Rollback plan for the launch itself** — distinct from Slice 13's workflow-cutover rollback

---

## Sequencing

1. **L2 list first** — CC produces the real backlog before anything is scheduled
2. **L1 CB smoke** — the findings feed L2
3. **L2 burn-down** — PDF blockers first; they're customer-facing
4. **L1 second pass** by a real PM, after the burn-down
5. **L3 training**, once the flow is stable
6. **L4 launch prep**

---

## Close criteria

- A PM who has never seen Nexus can complete a quote lifecycle using only the training material
- Zero known customer-facing defects
- CB's full-lifecycle smoke passes clean
- Every backlog item is either fixed or explicitly deferred with a reason
- Production credentials verified; rollback plan written

---

## Note on the pattern

Three slices' worth of evidence says the same thing: **independent verification finds what the builder's own suites do not.** Ten findings on Step 7, seven on 8b, six on 8c-4 — every one after green tsc, green prebuild, and green smoke.

Slice 14 should be resourced on that basis. The walk is not a formality at the end; it is the step that finds the problems.

"""### 🔴 ITEM GROUPS — the earlier conclusion was WRONG. Path REOPENED.

**⚠️ Read the correction at the end of this block before acting on the table below.**""")

s=s.replace(
"""**NOT YET TESTED — the next probe:** a **three-step attachment** — POST the SO with flat lines, then **PATCH** to add or replace with a group line, then PATCH member rates. Every attempt so far put the group on at **create** time; PATCH on a **saved** record is a different validator path, and it mirrors what Aisha actually does. If it works, the grouped SO comes back with no RESTlet and no migration.""",
"""### ✅ THE CORRECTION — Probes 6 and 7 falsified the above

**Edward pushed back on accepting the conclusion:** *"that doesn't sound like an API limitation."* He was right, and it nearly cost us the feature.

**The error meant exactly what it said.** `"Please enter a value for Amount"` is about a MISSING FIELD, not an architectural refusal. The validator computes member amounts from each member's **item-level `/price`** at parse time, BEFORE reading any inline rate on the line. DPS's catalogue items have no `/price` — so it fails.

**Definitive evidence:**
| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Bare group POST, member **with** `/price` | **204 CREATED** |
| Bare group POST, member **without** `/price` | 400, the familiar error |
| Group POST + inline member rates, unpriced members | 400 — inline rates are never reached |
| **`PATCH /salesOrder/{id}/item/{lineIdx}` `{rate: X}`** | **204 — updates the expanded member line IN PLACE** |

**So the working sequence is:** `POST bare group → GET expandSubResources → PATCH each member line with the quote's real rate`. **`$0.00` satisfies the validator** — semantically honest here, since DPS builds custom products and has no price until supplier costing returns.

**Vu relocated the fix upstream:** NetSuite items are unpriced because the **HubSpot products** are unpriced. *"All prices should be carried over to NetSuite if it is available in HubSpot."*

**⛔ TWO HAZARDS — requirements, not cautions, since this lands on the irreversible step:**
- **Sublist PATCH returns 204 while SILENTLY DUPLICATING** the group expansion. Doubled rollup, **no error** — a wrong SO that reports success. Only single-line PATCH is safe. **Must be structurally impossible in code.**
- **Partial failure mid-sequence** leaves the SO created, group expanded, some members priced and some at `$0` — a valid record with wrong amounts and nothing flagging it. Needs **read-back verification** before marking the push succeeded.

**Per-SO call count: 1 → 8–12.**

**STATUS: required for 1.0 per Edward. Now Slice 13 R2**, with three routes (HubSpot backfill / Vu's direct NetSuite update / RESTlet). None blocked.

**The banked lesson — `#155`:** *a thorough elimination is not a diagnosis.* Seven payload shapes across two API surfaces looked definitive. The conclusion drawn from it was wrong. **When a system rejects something, explain the stated reason before accepting any conclusion built on it.**""")

open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")

# CA → CC — #156: **CONDITIONAL GREEN.** Item 2 disposition below.

`advance-target.ts` with `computeUmbrellaAdvance(currentTab, quoteStatus)` is the right fix — one derivation, five consumers, and returning null when the tab *is* the frontier so it keeps its own submit action is a clean way to avoid parallel wiring. That's a pattern fix, not an instance fix.

Item 6 rounding at the source in both actions, with every downstream boundary inheriting it, is better than rounding at each call site. And confirming the NetSuite payload was already `toFixed(4)` closes the question I raised.

## Item 2 — **rename, and you were right to hold it**

`netsuite_so_pushed` is the outlier. Every other lifecycle action names the transition — `quote_sent`, `quote_accepted`, `quote_reverted`, `quote_revised`. This one names the mechanism.

**Rename to `quote_completed`.** Three reasons:

1. **The audit log records what happened to the quote**, not how. If the mechanism changes — and it may, since Item Groups reopening means `markComplete` could grow a multi-call sequence — the action name would become wrong while the transition stayed the same.
2. **The brief already specifies `quote_completed`.** It's in Step 9's own scope line and in the watch items. The convention didn't drift by accident; the implementation just got ahead of it.
3. **Now is the only cheap moment.** Renaming an audit action after production data exists means either a migration or a permanent two-name history.

**How, and this matters:** are there existing `netsuite_so_pushed` rows? Every one I know of came from smoke fixtures that were cleaned up. **Confirm the count is zero before renaming** — if any survive, we need a migration rather than a code change, and I'd want to see them first.

**Keep the `diff_json` payload as-is.** The mechanism detail belongs in the payload, and it's good — `accepted_tier_id_before/after`, `override_applied`, `retry_outcome`, `amount_pushed`. Only the action name changes.

**Not dual-row.** Two rows for one transition is worse than either single option — it doubles the log for no information gain and makes "what happened to this quote" a query rather than a read.

**Your instinct to hold rather than quietly fix was correct.** The finding tells us something: the convention slipped at exactly the moment the mechanism felt more important than the state. Worth a line in the CLAUDE.md banks — *name audit actions after the transition, not the mechanism, especially when the mechanism is the interesting part.*

## Accepted

Items 1, 3, 4, 5, 6. Two `disabled={pending}` textarea violations found and removed is a real Pattern 47 catch — the verifier newly passing means it was actually broken, not just unverified.

---

**Rename, confirm the row count is zero, then merge.** That closes Step 9 and leaves only Step 10 in Slice 12.

# CA → CD — Step 10 Designer Audit (R9.1)

Slice 12 is built. All of R9.1's surfaces shipped, and Nexus now creates real NetSuite Sales Orders end to end — verified by an independent smoke walk on a live send.

**This is an audit, not a design round.** Compare what shipped against your canonical design and tell us where it drifted. Two open questions at the end.

## What to audit

**Sub-tab 4 (Acceptance)** and **sub-tab 5 (Sales Order)** as built, against `app/r9/ceremony.jsx` and `app/r9/styles.css`.

- Structural fidelity to the canonical prototype
- CSS adopted verbatim per Pattern 30, addendum layered over r8, no reinterpretation
- **Your seven load-bearing items** — did they survive implementation? Particularly the choice/commitment split, the deliberate handoff, the heavy/light asymmetry, and HubSpot failure staying outside any modal

## Nexus adaptations — accept or flag as drift

Each was deliberate and is documented in the fidelity manifest. We need your read on whether any crossed into drift:

1. **`failed_at: 'item_group' | 'so_create'` discriminator** — added at CA's request so the failed state could specialize on which half of a two-operation push failed. **Then dropped**, because the shipped payload uses flat lines and never creates an Item Group. Header comment states it returns if the grouped path reopens.
2. **`soId` / `soCreatedAt` as nullable props**, not tied to the send action's return. Built when the SO might have been asynchronous. It isn't — but the shape was kept in case it becomes so.
3. **Two-reason disabled shape** on the CTA — `stubDisabled || belowFloor`, with an aggregated reason. R9 has one disable reason.
4. **`"ready to send"`** on the lock tab in `done` state. R9 emits `"done · revisitable"` universally, but never renders the lock tab in `done` — your linear model has no tab after it. Nexus's Revise re-entry surfaces the state. `"done · revisitable"` would be false under Pattern 52.
5. **`other`** added to the channel picker — schema supports it; your fixture ships email/call/portal only.
6. **Dev switcher via URL params** rather than the tweaks panel, guarded to non-production.

## One thing that did NOT ship, and it's customer-visible

**Item Groups are not automated.** Nexus emits flat SO lines with correct prices; Aisha still wraps them into an Item Group by hand for anything a customer sees.

Not a design failure — NetSuite's API refuses a group line unless every member carries an item-level price, and DPS's catalogue has none. We've since found the route and it's required for 1.0, but it lands in the next slice.

**No UI consequence** — the grouping is invisible to the PM either way. Flagging it so the audit isn't conducted against an assumption that it's done.

## Two questions from the independent smoke walk

These came from someone encountering your design cold, with no knowledge of the reasoning behind it.

**1. The two retry buttons in the failed state.**

Flagged across **two separate walks**: *"a small 'Retry send' button inside the red box, and a large 'Retry — send order to NetSuite' at the bottom — both greyed, both presumably doing the same thing, with no indication whether they differ."*

Both are canonical (`ceremony.jsx:118, 443, 594`), so we kept them per Pattern 30 rather than overruling your design. But a repeated usability signal from a fresh reader deserves your response. **Intentional redundancy, or worth consolidating?**

**2. Should the receipt surface a divergence between the transcribed note and the captured tier?**

Sub-tab 4 captures the customer's words *and* the tier the PM selected. Nothing on screen reconciles them.

Our smoke fixture accidentally contained a mismatch — the note read "Tier 2, 10k units" while the captured tier was 5,000 — and the walker caught it, noting that *"nothing on screen reconciles or even acknowledges that gap."*

A real transcription error would be invisible. **Is that a gap worth designing for**, or is the PM re-reading their own transcription sufficient?

## One thing your design got right, confirmed independently

You dropped the typed `FINALIZE` gate, arguing that a full order receipt carries more weight than a confirmation ritual — *weight through comprehension beats weight through obstruction* — with the condition that thinning the receipt brings the gate back.

The independent walker, hitting that dialog cold before an irreversible action: **"this is the best-communicated irreversible-action warning I've seen in this app across all walks."**

The trade was right.

## Deliverable

An audit report, not a design round. Flag drift, answer the two questions, and tell us if anything needs redesign — in which case that's scoped separately.

# Step 10 · Designer audit — R9.1 as built **Scope:** sub-tabs 4 (Acceptance) and 5 (Sales Order), shipped Slice 12, against `app/r9/ceremony.jsx` + `app/r9/styles.css`. **Verdict:** **no redesign required.** Six adaptations reviewed — five accepted, one watch item. Two smoke-walk questions answered: **question 1 is a real defect and it's mine**; **question 2 is a genuine gap worth designing** (small, scoped below). --- ## 1 · Load-bearing items — survival check All nine (seven from §6, plus 8 and 9 added in R9.1) survive. | # | Item | Status | |---|---|---| | 1 | Tier choice at capture, commitment at the lock | ✅ intact — two columns, `accepted_tier_id` NULL until send | | 2 | Deliberate handoff, no auto-navigation into sub-tab 5 | ✅ intact | | 3 | Heavy/light asymmetry | ✅ intact — slab + dark-header confirm, no gate | | 4 | HubSpot failure outside any modal, on sub-tab 4 | ✅ intact | | 5 | Rollback + revise visible as peers | ✅ intact | | 6 | Now/Later system cards | ✅ intact | | 7 | Override behind a disclosure naming the contradiction | ✅ intact | | 8 | The order receipt (replaced the typed gate) | ✅ intact — full lines, totals, ledger. **Condition still binding:** thin it and the gate returns. | | 9 | Failed state stays a tab, never a modal | ✅ intact | Structural fidelity and the addendum discipline hold: r9 layered over r8, five documented overrides, nothing merged edited. ## 2 · Nexus adaptations — accept / drift **Accepted, not drift (5):** 1. **`failed_at` discriminator added then dropped.** Correct. It specialized on a distinction the shipped payload can't produce; carrying dead branching in a load-bearing failure surface is worse than removing it. Header comment naming the reopen condition is exactly right. 2. **Two-reason disabled shape (`stubDisabled || belowFloor`) with aggregated reason.** Accepted. The caption's job is to tell the PM *why* they can't proceed; aggregation preserves that. R9 had one reason because the prototype had no stub state. 3. **`other` in the channel picker.** Accepted — schema supports it and a channel enum without an escape hatch forces mis-filing. My fixture was illustrative. 4. **Dev switcher via URL params, non-production guarded.** Accepted and preferred. `.r8-proto` was flagged prototype-only, strip in production — this honours it. 5. **`"ready to send"` on the lock tab in `done`.** Accepted, and it's a correct catch: my `subFor` emits `"done · revisitable"` universally, which under Pattern 52 would be false — nothing after the lock is revisitable. My linear model never rendered that combination; Nexus's Revise re-entry does. *Minor copy suggestion, not drift:* in `done` the order is already placed, so **`"order placed"`** reads truer than `"ready to send"` (which describes the pending state). Use whichever, but don't revert to `"done · revisitable"`. **Watch item (1):** 6. **`soId` / `soCreatedAt` as nullable props not tied to the send return.** Accepted as a shape, but flagging one coupling. Canonically the receipt keys its header stamp on **state**, not on SO-id presence: ``` placed ?
{netsuite.so_id}
:
no order number yet
``` If the shipped component keys that stamp (or the ledger's NetSuite row) on `soId != null` instead, then any state where the SO exists but the prop hasn't resolved renders **"no order number yet" on a placed order** — a receipt asserting something false about itself. Please confirm the stamp and the ledger both derive from state. If the SO ever does become asynchronous, that's a new state on the ledger (`creating…`), not a nullable stamp. ## 3 · Item Groups not automated — accepted, one note No UI consequence for the PM; the audit isn't affected. One thing to record, though: it puts the **receipt and the customer's artifact out of alignment** — the PM signs flat lines, the customer receives grouped ones. That's adjacent to map item 10 (the receipt must reconcile to what the customer and CRM see). Prices match, so nothing is *wrong* today. But when grouping automates, the receipt should render the grouped shape, because a receipt's authority comes from matching what was actually sent. Worth carrying into the next slice rather than discovering later. ## 4 · Question 1 — the two retry buttons **Not intentional redundancy. It's a defect, and it's mine.** Both call `setModal(true)` with no difference in behaviour — `ceremony.jsx:443` (in the red half) and `:594` (advance bar). Two identically-named controls for one action, and the walker flagged it twice. Pattern 30 was honoured correctly here; the canonical design was wrong. **Fix — consolidate to the advance bar.** Remove the in-box `Retry send`; keep `Copy error` there. Reasoning: every forward action in the umbrella lives in the advance bar, and the retry *is* the forward action — same button, same slab, relabelled. The split banner's job is to **explain** (two facts, equal weight), not to act; giving it a CTA duplicated the act and diluted its explanatory job. Load-bearing item 9 is unaffected — the error still lives on the tab, not in a modal. One related thing to check: the walker saw **both greyed**. Canonically the in-box button has no `disabled` prop; only the advance bar carries `disabled={blocked || pushing}`. If the shipped in-box button is disabled by the same condition, that's an added coupling — moot once it's removed, but it suggests the disable predicate got applied broadly. Worth confirming a blocked-below-floor state still leaves `Copy error` live. **Scope:** delete one button, one CSS rule unaffected. Not a design round. ## 5 · Question 2 — note-vs-tier divergence **A real gap, and worth designing for.** Your fixture reproduced the exact failure mode by accident, which is the strongest possible evidence: a transcription error is currently invisible, and it propagates into an irreversible NetSuite order. It's also the same problem R8 already solved once. The **sent-vs-draft mismatch banner** exists because two facts that ought to agree (what you sent, what you've edited) were displayed apart, so I built a surface that states the disagreement in the PM's own terms. Note-vs-tier is that pattern again, one tab over — and I missed it because I designed the capture as a *transcription* and never asked what happens when the transcription and the selection disagree. **Proposed treatment — a light, non-blocking reconciliation notice.** Deliberately modest: - **Detection:** scan the note for tier and quantity tokens (`tier 2`, `T2`, `10k`, `10,000 units`) and compare against the captured tier. Token match only — no natural language understanding, no inference from prose. - **Surface:** when they disagree, a quiet inline notice directly under the tier chips — *"Your note mentions Tier 2 · 10,000 units. You've selected T1 · 5,000 units."* Plus the two readings side by side. Warn register, not error. - **Never blocks.** The PM may legitimately be recording a customer who said one thing and agreed to another. The notice asks; it does not gate. Same principle as the override disclosure: state the contradiction, let the human decide. - **Silent when they agree, and when no tokens are found.** Most notes won't parse, and a notice that fires on ambiguity would train PMs to ignore it. - **A second home on the receipt** is optional and I'd argue against it: the receipt's authority comes from being about the *order*, and the divergence is about the *transcription*. Catch it at capture, where it's still cheap. **Scope:** one detection helper, one notice component, ~one CSS block. Small, but it is new design — flag it as its own mini-round rather than folding it into the audit. ## 6 · Confirmed Nothing else needs redesign. The FINALIZE trade is recorded as holding, with item 8's reversal condition intact — if the receipt is ever thinned, the gate comes back. **Actions out of this audit:** 1. Delete the in-box `Retry send` (defect, mine) — trivial. 2. Confirm the header stamp + ledger derive from state, not `soId` nullability. 3. Optional: `"order placed"` over `"ready to send"` in the lock tab's `done` state. 4. Note-vs-tier reconciliation notice — scope as a separate mini-round. 5. Carry receipt/Item-Group alignment into the grouping slice.

- Only `mark-complete.ts` (lines 528-538, 651-652) writes `netsuiteSoPushStatus` / `netsuiteSoPushError` / `netsuiteSoTranid`; `mark-complete.ts:109` guards `quote.status !== "accepted"` (rejects on 'complete')
- Freeze-tx (642-696) writes all 6 Slice 12 columns in one UPDATE; runs on 'accepted' quotes only
- `assertDraft` (quotes.ts:213) called at 9 sites in quotes.ts; NONE include the netsuite columns in their edit surface
- No canonical "freeze list" inventory exists in one place — it's implicit across schema comments

**Assessment:** The freeze list is complete for the mechanism operating today. The 3 new mirror columns (`netsuiteSoTranid`, `netsuiteSoPushStatus`, `netsuiteSoPushError`) ARE effectively frozen post-complete because nothing except `mark-complete.ts` writes them, and `mark-complete.ts` rejects non-accepted quotes at STEP 1. But this is architecturally identical to Pattern 52's stated failure mode: reproducibility guaranteed by convention, not by `assertDraft` on the mutation entry.

The failure surface: Slice 13+ admin surface (e.g., "retry failed SO push", "manually record NetSuite SO id"), NetSuite reconcile job, or a Slice 15 CS support tool — any of these could write these columns without knowing to fail-closed against `status='complete'`. Same risk as the base Pattern 52 columns.

- **RECOMMEND**: Add a canonical freeze-list inventory to `docs/BOM_NOTES.md` or a new `docs/pattern-52-freeze-list.md`. Enumerate all 30 columns (27 CA identified + `netsuiteSoTranid` + `netsuiteSoPushStatus` + `netsuiteSoPushError`). Cross-reference from Pattern 52 in CLAUDE.md. Cost of adding: 1 hour. Cost of missing this AT Slice 13 admin build: the same debugging round we've already seen for missing FK behavior.
- **RECOMMEND**: When Slice 13 admin surfaces are briefed, `§0.5` includes an explicit "does this write any Pattern 52 column?" check. If yes, action must call an `assertRevisable(quote)` helper that fails on `status IN ('accepted', 'complete')` for anything except the sanctioned reopen path.
- **OK**: Current writers respect the freeze by construction.

## 3. Choice/commitment FK pair

**Evidence:**
- FK asymmetry verified: `customer_accepted_tier_id → ... SET NULL`; `accepted_tier_id → ... RESTRICT`
- Freeze-tx writes `acceptedTierId: effectiveAcceptedTierId` (mark-complete.ts:647). Precedence `quote.acceptedTierId ?? quote.customerAcceptedTierId` (127-128) — override wins; v1 no-override always falls back.
- `deleteTier` (quotes.ts:918-947) has `assertDraft` guard; tier delete blocked on any non-draft quote — RESTRICT is defense in depth only
- 1 accepted quote (customer_set, accepted NULL), 0 complete quotes — no live post-freeze evidence

**Assessment:** Design intent survives. Post-freeze the RESTRICT locks tier deletion via DB constraint; `assertDraft` locks it via app layer. `customer_accepted_tier_id` staying at SET NULL preserves history-forgiving semantics for the customer's declared choice (nice-to-preserve, not load-bearing forensic). The asymmetry — one SET NULL, one RESTRICT — makes structural sense: the customer's stated choice is data; the commitment is contract.

**BLOCKER-adjacent finding — `netsuite_so_pushes.accepted_tier_id` has NO FK constraint** (0045 line 14: `"accepted_tier_id" uuid NOT NULL,` — no `REFERENCES`). If a tier row is deleted out-of-band (data admin cleanup), the push row's `accepted_tier_id` becomes an orphan uuid. Today the app layer's `assertDraft` blocks tier delete on accepted/complete quotes, so the app can't cause this. But defense-in-depth is thin.

- **RECOMMEND** (pre-launch, low-cost): Add `REFERENCES quote_tiers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT` to `netsuite_so_pushes.accepted_tier_id`. Single-line migration; no data migration needed (all current values are valid — 0 rows). Symmetric with `quotes.accepted_tier_id` RESTRICT semantics. Migration destination: new manual `0047_netsuite_so_pushes_fk_tighten.sql`.
- **OK**: Choice/commitment split holds correctly against live evidence.

## 4. New tables

**`netsuite_item_groups` (0 rows):**
- Shape supports the three Slice 13 reactivation routes (a/b/c per UX_BACKLOG). `composition_hash` key + per-customer scope + `netsuite_external_id` unique are correct for all three.
- **Concern:** `firstUsedByQuoteId → quotes ON DELETE SET NULL` — same shape as SoPushes but this table is intended long-lived (per CA "groups are historically anchored"). If a quote is deleted (draft cleanup), the row keeps the group but loses provenance. Design is acceptable but note that `first_used_by_deal_id` is bare `text` — no FK to `projects.hubspot_deal_id`, so it's stable across quote/project deletes. Good.
- **BANK**: If Slice 13 reactivates, the description-generation path exists but is untested against real production items. Sandbox smoke covers happy path only.
- **OK**: Shape is right for reactivation; zero live weight until then.

**`netsuite_so_pushes` (0 rows currently):**
- Fresh INSERT per attempt design (mark-complete.ts:606-619) means N failures × M quotes produces N×M rows. UX_BACKLOG "Smoke-generated audit rows leave orphans" flags this at the audit_log level; same shape applies here.
- Partial unique index `WHERE status='succeeded'` correctly permits N failed rows per (quote, tier). Retry convergence path in mark-complete.ts (335-346, 372-393) works: CHECK-then-insert reads succeeded rows to bypass NetSuite POST.
- **`payload_snapshot jsonb`** is never pruned; each row carries the full SO request body. At production scale (say 5 SO pushes/mo, ~5KB each) storage is trivial. At 500/mo × 20KB = 10 MB/mo, still trivial. But no retention policy exists.
- **RECOMMEND**: Bank a payload_snapshot retention story in UX_BACKLOG. Suggest: after 90 days for succeeded pushes, null the `payload_snapshot` column (keep the row for forensic). Not urgent — bank as "Slice 14 or v1.1 admin hygiene." Do NOT ship now; premature per Pattern 32 tolerance until real production accumulates.
- **OK**: Shape is sound.

**`netsuite_customer_map` (9 rows):**
- Historical-anchor design: no delete path, all edits go through changed-audit. Consistent with the "map is contract" framing.
- PK on `hubspot_company_id` means a HubSpot company id renaming/reassignment path (rare but possible) would strand the mapping. Zero risk today; would surface if HubSpot admin ever merges two companies.
- **OK**: Shape is sound for v1.

## 5. Migration integrity

**Evidence:**
- `_journal.json` tracks auto-migrations 0-45 (46 entries) sequentially
- Live `__drizzle_migrations` has 38 rows, ids 7-47, gaps at 19/20/24 — first 7 auto-migrations were applied pre-tracking (early Slice 1 direct psql)
- Manual/0045 exists AND auto/0045 exists with same DDL; manual is idempotent (IF NOT EXISTS), auto is not
- Manual/0036 (data-fix: HubSpot stage label) and manual/0037 (data-fix: HubSpot stage ID key) collide numerically with auto-tracked DDL migrations of the same numbers
- Manual/0046 is a data-fix (tax code) with no auto-migration counterpart
- No manifest tracks which manual migrations have been applied to which environment — oral knowledge only

**Assessment: BLOCKER for production launch confidence.**

Concrete failure scenarios:
1. **Fresh deployment on a new Supabase project (or full DB reset)**: `drizzle-kit migrate` runs 0-45. Manual/0036, manual/0037, manual/0046 don't run automatically. HubSpot integration silently fails at markAccepted (wrong stage label / stage-ID key mismatch); NetSuite SO push fails with tax code error. All three are runtime-symptomatic, not startup-symptomatic. PMs discover the outage in the wild.
2. **New developer onboarding**: Same failure mode. No signal that manual migrations exist unless they read this specific CLAUDE.md.
3. **Prod rebuild required**: The order of "apply manual/0045 vs auto/0045" is ambiguous — auto/0045 is not idempotent (CREATE TABLE without IF NOT EXISTS at line 1); manual/0045 is idempotent. If someone runs the auto tool after the manual tool, prod errors.

- **BLOCKER**: Before v1 launch, either (a) reconcile manual/0036/0037/0046 into a proper drizzle-tracked migration OR (b) add an explicit `scripts/apply-all-manual.mjs` that reads a manifest file listing which manual migrations must be applied at any deployment. Preferred: (a) — collapse manual/0036 into auto-drizzle-kit's model. Manual/0046 (tax code data fix) can be idempotent SQL in a new auto/0047 migration.
- **BLOCKER-adjacent**: manual/0045 vs auto/0045 duplication — pick one, delete the other. Since auto/0045 is already in `_journal.json` and applied to prod, delete manual/0045 or leave it explicitly marked "obsolete — auto/0045 supersedes."

## 6. Speculative additions

**`pendingHubspotFromStageId` + `pendingHubspotFromStageVersion` (0 rows populated):**
- Defensive engineering against a REAL failure mode (from_stage poisoning on retry after HubSpot succeeds + DB tx fails). Zero rows means either no failures happened, or every failure completed retry successfully (clearing the columns).
- The pattern is textbook Pattern 52 sibling: pre-write outside tx, clear inside tx that finalizes state. Cost: 2 nullable columns + 1 extra UPDATE per accept attempt. Benefit: rollback via unmarkAccepted reads correct from_stage on ANY retry outcome.
- **Keep as-is.** This is exactly the kind of correctness cost that Slice 12 should have paid. Removing pre-launch would trade a real bug for two columns.
- **OK**.

**`netsuite_item_groups` (0 rows):**
- Assessed in §4. Shape is right for reactivation. `smoke:netsuite-item-groups` script keeps the primitives exercised.
- **OK — keep**. Removing pre-Slice-13 would require re-shipping when Vu's backfill lands.

---

## Standing-cost analysis (production-hardening lens)

Ranked by cost of change once Nexus is in production use:

1. **Manual migration model** (§5 BLOCKER). Once prod carries real deals, "we need to re-apply manual/0037 to a hot DB" is a real production incident. Fix cost NOW: ~2 hours to collapse into auto-migrations + document. Fix cost POST-LAUNCH: same 2 hours + downtime coordination + risk of running on a DB with partial state.

2. **Pattern 52 freeze list held by convention** (§2 RECOMMEND). Once Slice 13 or admin/reconcile paths land, any new writer could bypass without knowing. Fix cost NOW: 1 hour to enumerate + add an `assertRevisable` helper. Fix cost POST-LAUNCH: potentially data corruption on completed quotes that requires audit reconstruction to unwind.

3. **`netsuite_so_pushes.accepted_tier_id` missing FK** (§3 RECOMMEND). Symptom: orphan uuid in forensic table if tier deleted out-of-band. Fix cost NOW: 1-line migration. Fix cost POST-LAUNCH: data cleanup of orphans + backfill FK integrity check.

4. **`payload_snapshot` retention** (§4 BANK). Storage growth is gentle; won't matter for 6-12 months at v1 scale. Fix cost NOW or later: same. Genuine BANK.

5. **`netsuiteSoId varchar(50)` vs `netsuiteSoTranid text` type asymmetry** (§1 BANK). Cosmetic. Fix in any future migration that touches the columns.

6. **Stale `customer_accepted_tier_id` on unmark → revise path** (§1 BANK). Not customer-visible today. Would become a real issue only if a future admin surface reads it out of context. BANK.

The three items worth resolving pre-launch (in order): the manual-migration reconciliation (#1) is the only true BLOCKER — the other two RECOMMENDs are worth 2-3 hours to close but wouldn't block v1 launch if deferred.

Reference paths:
- `src/lib/netsuite/mark-complete.ts` (freeze-tx entrance, mirror-column writes)
- `src/app/actions/quotes.ts:213` (assertDraft), `:918-947` (deleteTier), `:2404-2519` (unmarkAccepted), `:1860-1935` (reviseFromAccepted)
- `src/db/schema.ts:305-544` (quotes), `:2257-2426` (netsuite tables)
- `drizzle/manual/0036_slice_12_step_7b_hubspot_stage_label_fix.sql`, `0037_...`, `0045_...`, `0046_...` (unreconciled manual migrations)
- `drizzle/0045_slice_12_step_8c3_schema.sql:14` (missing FK on `accepted_tier_id`)

# CB Smoke Brief — Full Quote Umbrella Walk

*(Paste-ready. Sign-in: hand CB a signed-in session.)*

**⚠️ The Send button is LIVE and this walk includes completing it.** It creates a real order in a real system.

---

This is the final walk of the quote umbrella before the slice closes. You've walked pieces of it before; this one covers **the whole thing in sequence**, including paths you haven't seen.

**Fixture:** `[CC provides — see requirements below]`

## Ground rules

1. **This writes to a production database and two live external systems.**
2. **Ask me before every state-changing click.** Wait for my go.
3. **Walk F (the send) is pre-approved** — complete it when you reach it.
4. **Do not fix, clean up, or retry anything.**
5. Browser only. Only touch the fixture quote.

---

## Walk A — A sent quote, from the start

Start at Preview Quote. Move through each tab in order: **Preview → Send to Client → Client Review → Acceptance → Sales Order.**

For each: what's on screen, what state the quote is in, what action is offered, what's greyed or locked.

**Watch for:** any tab whose label, button, or status disagrees with another tab about the same quote.

## Walk B — Revise from sent

From Client Review, use **Revise**.

- What state does the quote land in?
- **Is the quote number unchanged?** Lead with this if it isn't.
- Does the version indicator change?
- Are the review-log entries still there?
- What does the version picker show — is the previous version still listed?
- Which tabs are now reachable, and which aren't?

Then get the quote back to a sendable state and send it again. Report what that took.

## Walk C — Acceptance

On the Acceptance tab, record the acceptance: transcribe what the customer said, pick a tier, choose how it arrived.

- Is it clear what you're recording and what happens next?
- After recording — what changed on this tab, and across the strip?
- Check Client Review: did anything get logged automatically? Quote it.

## Walk D — Roll back the acceptance

Use **Roll back**.

- Does everything revert, or does anything linger?
- Does the review log show the rollback?
- Can you accept again cleanly?

## Walk E — Revise from accepted

Accept again, then use **Revise** rather than Roll back.

- Where does the quote end up?
- **Quote number still unchanged?**
- Anything that looks like it belongs to the previous state?

Then return to accepted.

## Walk F — Send the order

Go to Sales Order. **Report the screen before clicking anything** — order details, totals, status list, the button and its caption.

Click Send. **Report the confirmation dialog before pressing through**, then complete it.

After:
- Order number, timestamps, status list
- **Try clicking an earlier tab.** Does it actually do nothing?
- Is it obvious what happened and what can no longer be changed?

## Walk G — Alternate states (dev URLs, no clicks)

`&dev=1&so-flags=below_floor` · `&so-flags=unmatched` · `&so-flags=both` · `&so-state=failed` · `&so-state=record`

For each: does the whole screen agree with itself, and does the Send button reflect the condition?

---

## Report

**Answer directly:**

- **Did the quote number stay constant through every revise?**
- Did any number disagree with any other number, anywhere?
- Did any tab contradict another about the same quote's state?
- Any text mentioning build steps, phases, or pending work? Quote it.
- **Walking the whole lifecycle in one pass — did anything feel out of order, redundant, or like a step you'd expect and didn't get?**
- Anything ambiguous about what a button would do?

Flag small things. Odd wording, a number that looks off, a label that doesn't match its behaviour.

---

**CC — fixture requirements:** quote in **`sent`** state at the start, not accepted — CB needs to walk the full lifecycle. Throwaway HubSpot deal (zero line items, zero company associations), a `netsuite_customer_map` row so the send resolves, leaves that resolve to NetSuite items, tier above the floor, ≥1 review-feed entry. **The send creates a real sandbox SO — clean up after CB reports, scanning NetSuite directly per #152.**

That changes the finding materially — and it's worse than CB reported.

**There IS a confirmation. It's a native browser dialog.** CB didn't recognise it as part of the app because it isn't — `window.confirm()` renders as an OS-level box, unstyled, outside the page.

**Three problems with that:**

1. **Inconsistency.** Every other confirm in the umbrella is an in-app modal with itemized consequences, a named cancel path, and copy stating what happens externally. This one is a system alert.
2. **It can't say what a real modal says.** `window.confirm()` takes a plain string — no formatting, no consequence list, no "this moves the deal back to Development & Quoting" laid out properly. The action with the least explanation is the one touching a live CRM.
3. **Browsers suppress it.** Repeated dialogs from the same page get a "prevent this page from creating additional dialogs" checkbox. Once ticked, **the confirm silently stops appearing** and rollback becomes a one-click live write with no guard. That's a real failure mode, not theoretical.

**And CB is a useful signal here:** someone walking the app carefully didn't register it as a confirmation at all. It reads as a browser interruption, not a decision point.

---

**This should be a sweep, not a fix.** Adding as **Q8**:

> **Audit every confirmation in the app for `window.confirm` / `alert` / `prompt`.** Rollback uses one. Others may too — the umbrella's modals are consistent, but Setup, Costs, and Pricing haven't been reviewed for this and haven't been walked since Slice 11.

> **Replace all with in-app modals** matching the established pattern: name the action, itemize consequences, state external effects, give an explicit cancel.

**Worth noting for the readiness conversation:** this is a case where the *pattern* was right everywhere it was designed, and wrong where nobody designed it. CD specified the ceremonial confirms; rollback got a default. That's the shape of gap that a written standard would catch and a per-PR review doesn't.

**What's wrong:** the confirmation is an inline panel appended below the receipt, not a modal. Consequences:

**Two competing "Send" buttons on screen at once.** The panel's `Send order to NetSuite` and the sticky advance bar's `Send order to NetSuite` — both visible, both live-looking. On the irreversible action. A PM could press either, and there's no way to tell from looking whether they do the same thing.

Right, and this is a gap in the design's assumptions, not just a missing feature.

The whole reversibility model treats the NetSuite push as the point of no return — *"the order is irreversible in the PM's hands. Cancel it in NetSuite."* That's technically accurate and operationally incomplete. The order can be voided in NetSuite. What can't be done is **getting Nexus back to a state that matches**.

**The mismatch is the actual problem.** After a void, NetSuite has no order, but Nexus still shows `complete`, holds `netsuite_so_id`, and has every column frozen. The quote is permanently locked to an order that no longer exists — and the PM can't revise, can't re-accept, can't re-send. The record lies, and there's no path back.

**What a documented process needs to cover:**

- **Who can authorize it**, and on what basis
- **The NetSuite side** — void or close, and whether either is reversible if the void was itself a mistake
- **The HubSpot side** — the deal is at Won with an amount; does it move back?
- **The Nexus side** — this is the part with no answer today. An admin action that unfreezes, clears the NetSuite columns, and returns the quote to `accepted`, with an audit row recording who, when, and why
- **What the customer sees** — if a revised quote follows, is it a new version, and does the number still hold
- **Ordering** — almost certainly NetSuite first, then Nexus, so we never unfreeze a quote whose order still exists

**Two things worth naming now:**

The R9 design already gestured at this — *"an admin can unlock the quote with a reason"* — and we **deferred it**, then removed the button because it pointed at nothing. So the need was identified during design and dropped for scope. Worth recording that it wasn't an oversight.

And it interacts with Q13. If completed quotes are reachable by URL with live forms, then an *undocumented* unlock path effectively exists already — just a broken one. Fixing the lock and building the unlock are the same conversation.

Adding to Slice 13 as **R7 — Sales Order reversal**. Process first, then whatever code it needs.

Understood — and that's the correct posture while Nexus isn't in production. Nothing should reach a customer from a system under test.

**But it means "Send to Client" is currently a name for something else.** What it does is generate the PDF, snapshot the terms, assign the number, and mark the quote sent. The PM then delivers it manually — presumably by downloading and emailing themselves.

**Which is fine, as long as it's the stated design.** The problem is the interface doesn't say so. *"Sent — awaiting [customer]"* and *"Quote v2 sent to edward@thedps.co"* both imply delivery happened. A PM who doesn't know better would wait for a reply to something that was never sent.

**So the question isn't whether to build email — it's what v1 claims.** Three options:

1. **Delivery is manual by design for v1.** Then the copy should say so: *"Quote ready to send"* rather than *"Sent"*, and the confirmation should tell the PM to download and send it. Honest, and no new capability needed.
2. **Email ships in v1** but is disabled until launch. Then it's a stub with a switch, and it needs to work before go-live.
3. **Manual permanently.** Then "Send to Client" is the wrong name for the tab and should change.

**My read:** option 1 is likely right for v1 — you're not blocked on it, PMs already have email, and building delivery adds bounce handling, tracking, and a deliverability surface nobody's asked for.

**But the copy has to match**, because the whole lifecycle keys off `sent` and the PM's mental model of what happened.

**Reframing R8:** the inventory isn't just "what's unbuilt" — it's **where the interface claims more than the system does.** Email is the clearest case, and it's not a bug. It's an undeclared design decision.

Worth deciding which of the three options v1 ships with, since it changes copy across several surfaces.

No fetch path exists anywhere in the codebase — grep across src/lib/netsuite/ for tranid retrieval returns three hits, all documentation confirming "caller can fetch separately" and none actually doing so.

salesOrderInternalId = created.internalId;
salesOrderTranid = null; // caller can fetch tranId separately if needed

cd /home/claude && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='SLICE-13-READINESS-SCOPE.md'
s=open(p).read()

anchor = "## Also in scope"

new = """## R6 — SO field parity completion · owner: CC + business input

The Step 10 field-parity probe (`scripts/parity/so-field-parity.ts`) diffed a Nexus-created SO against workflow-created reference **SO2646** and found **18 missing / 8 wrong** on an order that otherwise looked correct — right total, right lines, right status.

**Two were fixed in Slice 12** because they were guaranteed failures:
- `shipDate` defaulted to *today* on every order
- `custbody_dps_project_source` sent a text label to a list field — **NetSuite rejects it outright.** Any real deal with `sourcing_location` populated would fail at the POST. Caught only because Class B was re-run against a realistic cache row.

**Four remain, all needing business input rather than code decisions:**

| Field | Question |
|---|---|
| **`shipOverride` + `shipAddress`** | **Edward: per-deal ship-to override is the NORM.** Nexus currently relies on the customer's default address — so **most orders would ship to the wrong place.** Source unknown; the deal's "Final Ship To Information" section is the likely candidate. **Highest-stakes item in the slice.** |
| `otherRefNum` / `checkNumber` | The reference populates the *standard* NetSuite PO fields; we write only the custom one. Which does anything downstream read? |
| `custbody_dps_transaction_hold` | `true` on the reference; nobody knows the rule. Do not hardcode a business rule from a polluted sample — same lesson as the Project flag. |
| `custcol_dps_hubspot_line` | No natural value; Nexus doesn't source from HubSpot deal lines. Fabricate an index or drop. |

**Keep the parity probe as a standing gate** whenever `buildSalesOrderPayload` changes. It is the single most valuable artifact Step 10 produced.

---

## R7 — Sales Order reversal · owner: Edward + Melinda + Amy

**Edward: this happens. Humans make mistakes and there needs to be a documented way back.**

The design treats the NetSuite push as the point of no return — *"the order is irreversible in the PM's hands. Cancel it in NetSuite."* Technically accurate, operationally incomplete.

**The order can be voided in NetSuite. What cannot be done is getting Nexus back to a matching state.** After a void, NetSuite has no order, but Nexus still shows `complete`, holds `netsuite_so_id`, and has every Pattern 52 column frozen. The quote is permanently locked to an order that no longer exists — no revise, no re-accept, no re-send. **The record lies and there is no path back.**

**A documented process needs:**
- **Who authorises**, on what basis
- **NetSuite side** — void or close, and whether either is itself reversible
- **HubSpot side** — the deal sits at Won with an amount; does it move back?
- **Nexus side** — *no answer today.* An admin action that unfreezes, clears the NetSuite columns, returns the quote to `accepted`, and writes an audit row with who/when/why
- **Customer-facing** — if a revised quote follows, new version? Number still held?
- **Ordering** — NetSuite first, then Nexus, so we never unfreeze a quote whose order still exists

**Note:** R9 gestured at this — *"an admin can unlock the quote with a reason"* — and it was **deferred for scope**, then the button removed because it pointed at nothing. The need was identified during design and dropped. Not an oversight.

**Interacts with Q13:** completed quotes are currently reachable by URL with live forms, so an undocumented unlock path effectively exists already — just a broken one.

---

## R8 — Stub and capability inventory · owner: CC + Edward

**Edward: what was represented in the platform but never fully built out.**

Every one of these was caught by someone noticing, one at a time. **There is no inventory.**

| Found | Status |
|---|---|
| **Compare v1→v2** | Button present, tooltip admits it ships in v1.5+ |
| **View v{N} (sent)** | Present, disabled; capability exists, unwired |
| **"Request unlock (admin)"** | Pointed at nothing — removed in 8c-4 |
| **`so-failed-at` dev axis** | Parameter existed, did nothing |
| **Email delivery** | **See below** |

**The category is broader than unbuilt features.** A stub is anywhere the interface implies a capability the system lacks: controls that render but do nothing · actions that succeed locally without the external effect they claim · placeholders that look real (`TBC`, `SO-DEV-STUB`, `not-resolved-yet`) · copy describing unimplemented behaviour · fields captured but never consumed.

### The email question — an undeclared design decision, not a bug

**Send to Client does not email the customer.** Confirmed by Edward, and correct while Nexus isn't in production — nothing should reach a customer from a system under test.

**But the interface says otherwise.** The tab is called *Send to Client*, the state becomes `sent`, the log reads *"Quote v2 sent to…"*. A PM would mark a quote sent, wait for a response, and never learn the customer received nothing.

**Three options for v1 — pick one, because it changes copy across several surfaces:**
1. **Manual delivery by design.** Copy says so: *"Quote ready to send"*, and the confirmation tells the PM to download and send it. No new capability. **Likely right for v1.**
2. **Email ships in v1**, disabled until launch. Then it is a stub with a switch and must work before go-live.
3. **Manual permanently.** Then "Send to Client" is the wrong name for the tab.

**Deliverable:** every surface implying a capability, in three states — built and working · built but unwired · not built. Then per item: finish, remove, or label honestly.

---

"""
s = s.replace(anchor, new + anchor, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PYEOF

chat_messages.text:
**Nexus v2 — Progress Update 7/29/26**

**The headline: Nexus created a real Sales Order in NetSuite today, end to end.** A quote goes from accepted → Send → an order appears in NetSuite with the right customer, lines, prices, terms, and deal reference. That's the whole point of the last three weeks of work, and it's working.

**What shipped**

The full post-send lifecycle is now built: Preview → Send to Client → Client Review → Acceptance → Sales Order. A quote can be revised, rolled back, re-accepted, and revised again — keeping the same quote number throughout, so the customer never sees a different one. Acceptance pushes the deal to Won in HubSpot. Sending the order creates the NetSuite SO and locks the quote as the permanent record.

**What we learned — the NetSuite deep dive**

We spent a good chunk of yesterday and today scoping the NetSuite integration properly instead of building on assumptions. It changed the design more than once, and it was worth it.

**Thanks to Aisha, Melinda, Amy, Vu, and Cally** — this genuinely couldn't have been figured out from the outside. A few things we'd have gotten wrong:

- **Item Groups are templates, not priced records.** Components sit at $0; the real prices go on the order. We had it backwards.
- **NetSuite's API won't accept an Item Group on an order** the way the UI does — we tested every route. Turns out it needs a price on each component's item record first, which is why Aisha's manual step works and automation didn't. **That's a solvable problem and we're solving it.**
- **Projects, tax codes, and ship-to** all turned out to be handled by people, not by the system — so Nexus stays out of them.

**Where we are on grouping**

Right now Nexus creates the order with each component as its own line, priced correctly. **Aisha still wraps them into an Item Group by hand** for anything the customer sees. The prices are right, so it's a wrap rather than a re-entry — but it's not where we want to land, and item grouping is a requirement for v1. We have a path and we're working it.

**Testing**

We've been running independent walkthroughs of the app — someone going through it fresh with no knowledge of how it was built. Today's full-lifecycle walk found 15 things worth fixing, which is exactly what that process is for. Nothing structural; mostly wording, a couple of display bugs, and one screen that could be reached when it shouldn't be. All being fixed now.

**What's next**

Two more pieces of work before launch:

1. **Readiness** — finishing the item grouping, switching over from the current HubSpot automation, and closing out the last data gaps.
2. **Launch prep** — full testing, training materials, and a proper walkthrough with the team.

**Timing:** we're being deliberate about the remaining work rather than rushing it. I'll have a firmer date once the readiness scope is settled this week.

**Bottom line:** the hard part works. What's left is making it something the team can use without anyone having to know how it's built.

---

Two things you may want to adjust before posting:

**The 15 findings.** I framed them as routine, which they are — but "one screen that could be reached when it shouldn't be" is doing some work there. If this audience would rather hear it plainly, say so.

**The date.** I left it open rather than naming mid-August, since the readiness scope isn't settled and you've already moved it once. Your call whether an open date reads worse than a soft one.

- **Smoke-generated audit rows leave orphans on shared dev/prod DB
  (Slice 12 Step 9 CA finding, 2026-07-29).** The fixture cleanup
  script deliberately doesn't cascade to `audit_log` — that's
  correct for real audit trail forensic value. But every smoke run
  leaves permanent audit rows whose `entity_id` points at a
  deleted quote/project. Slice 12's two CB walks produced two
  orphan `quote_completed` rows (formerly `netsuite_so_pushed` —
  see rename); deleted manually as part of the Step 9 rename.
  Slice 13 and 14 will run many more.

  **Two paths, CA disposition banked:**
  - **Add a smoke marker.** Every smoke-fired action writes
    `diff_json.source = 'smoke_fixture'` (or a slice-scoped variant
    like `'smoke_cb_walk'`). Orphan rows are then filterable via
    `WHERE diff_json->>'source' = 'smoke_fixture'` — sweep them
    without touching production data. Pattern matches
    `initial_seed_8c3_post_merge` on `netsuite_customer_map` rows
    (Slice 12 Step 8c-3 seed).
  - **Cascade cleanup to audit_log.** Simpler but breaks the
    forensic-value guarantee for any real audit rows the cleanup
    accidentally sweeps.

  The marker approach is CA's lean — filterable-without-loss beats
  cascade-with-risk. Slice 14 L2 scope; not urgent.

## v1 readiness — pre-launch checklist items

(Items that must be verified before v1 ships. Not deferred polish;
operational pre-flight.)

- [Production DB connection-string posture]

  **Item:** Prod `DATABASE_URL` Vercel env var must point at
  Supabase **session-mode** pooler (port `:5432`), NOT
  transaction-mode pooler (port `:6543`).

  **Why:** transaction-mode pgbouncer multiplexing layer races
  postgres-js's response-correlation logic under concurrent
  `Promise.all` bursts (the `getCostingBundle` pattern). One
  query in the burst orphans; Vercel function hangs until timeout;
  page never renders. Full failure-mode signature + diagnostic
  ladder banked in CLAUDE.md ("Prod uses session-mode pooler
  (:5432), not transaction-mode (:6543)" section).

  **Verification:** at deploy time, confirm Vercel project env
  vars → Production → `DATABASE_URL` ends in `.pooler.supabase
  .com:5432/postgres?...` (not `:6543`). Pre-launch checklist
  + any env-var rotation procedure.

  **Banked from:** cell_ovr postmortem, 2026-06-17.

- [Production Supabase tier]

  **Item:** Production Supabase project on Pro tier ($25/mo) +
  at least Small compute add-on ($15/mo, 2 GB RAM + 2-core ARM
  CPU dedicated). Nano + Micro tiers are dev/preview only.

  **Why:** Nano + Micro share CPU with other tenants; catalog
  queries can stall for minutes under host load. Caused 2026-06-17
  production hang investigation.

  **Verification:** at deploy time, Supabase Dashboard → Project
  Settings → Compute → confirm tier ≥ Small.

  **Banked from:** 2026-06-17 production hang investigation.

- [Slice 11.5.1 — finish OLD-table drops + 5-file migration]

  **Item:** complete the OLD-model retirement that Slice 11.5
  Step 8 carved out. Five deeply-integrated files
  (warnings.ts engine, markup-defaults admin, sku-tree
  library, actions/quotes.ts legacy functions, quote-guards.ts
  helpers) need their OLD-schema reads migrated to NEW-model
  reads OR deleted; OLD tables then drop from `src/db/schema.ts`
  + drop migration applied to prod.

  **Why pre-launch (not v1.1+):** the Slice 11.5 brief's Q2
  wipe-and-reseed-at-launch posture eliminates OLD-table data.
  Once data is gone:
  - Legacy reads in those 5 files return empty
  - Either they break (NULL handling, type assumptions),
    render degraded (empty warnings / admin views), or work
    fine
  - We don't know which without verifying

  We can't safely wipe OLD tables at launch unless either
  (a) Slice 11.5.1 has shipped — files migrated to NEW model
  or deleted, OR (b) we explicitly confirm all 5 files
  gracefully handle empty OLD data. (a) is the safer, less
  archaeological path.

  **Verification:** Slice 11.5.1 ships pre-launch (not v1.1+
  per Edward's reclassification 2026-06-18). Slot in between
  Slice 11.5 close and Slice 11 audit, OR in parallel with
  Slice 12 external lead time. Half-day-to-day scope; cheap
  to absorb.

  **Banked from:** Slice 11.5 Step 8 carve (PR #73, 2026-06-18).

## Open

Read it. It's substantially better maintained than I assumed, and it changes two things about the Slice 13/14 docs I wrote.

**What I got wrong:** I built Slice 14's L2 as though I were assembling the backlog from memory. It already existed, structured, with explicit trigger conditions on the bank items — better discipline than my version. CC has been maintaining it properly throughout.

**What I didn't know about, and it matters:**

**`v1 readiness — pre-launch checklist`** contains three items neither of my docs mentions:

- **Production `DATABASE_URL` must use the session-mode pooler (`:5432`), not transaction-mode (`:6543`).** Transaction-mode races `postgres-js` under concurrent bursts — one query orphans, the function hangs until timeout, the page never renders. Banked from a real production postmortem in June.
- **Production Supabase on Pro tier + Small compute minimum.** Nano/Micro share CPU; catalog queries stall for minutes under host load. Also from a real incident.
- **Slice 11.5.1 — OLD-table drops + 5-file migration.** Explicitly reclassified pre-launch by you in June. Five files still read the OLD schema, and the wipe-and-reseed-at-launch posture means those reads return empty. **This is a carved-out slice of work classified as pre-launch that appears nowhere in my Slice 13 or 14 scope.**

That last one is the real gap. It's half-a-day-to-a-day of work, it's a launch blocker, and I'd have handed you two "complete" readiness documents without it.

**What I'd do:** rather than duplicating the backlog into my docs, point Slice 14's L2 at `UX_BACKLOG.md` as the source of truth and keep only the walk-specific framing. And add Slice 11.5.1 to Slice 13 or 14 explicitly — it's not readiness in the NetSuite sense, but it is pre-launch.

Worth me reconciling both docs against the backlog properly before the discussion?

content.text:
# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. The library `<script src>` tag must come BEFORE any inline script that uses its global — never call a library from code that appears above its `<script src>` tag. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Surfaces**: `--surface-2` (white), `--surface-1` (card), `--surface-0` (page bg); role tints `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Text**: `--text-primary` (black), `--text-secondary` (muted), `--text-muted` (hints); role `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Borders**: `--border` (default hairline), `--border-strong` (hover), `--border-stronger`; role `--border-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-voice` (serif), `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--radius` (8px), `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}`, `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}`; for larger corners use literal `12px`/`16px` All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--text-primary, --text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. Never use black, gray, or --text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes.
